subject: english-language
title: Idioms and what they really mean
summary: Common English idioms tested in WASSCE and UTME, and how to work out their meaning.

lesson.text: An idiom is a group of words whose meaning is different from the meanings of the separate words. "It's raining cats and dogs" has nothing to do with animals: it means it is raining heavily.

items: a piece of cake: very easy
burn the midnight oil: study or work late into the night
bury the hatchet: make peace after a quarrel
let the cat out of the bag: reveal a secret by mistake
break the ice: get people talking at the start of a meeting
beat about the bush: avoid saying the main point
take the bull by the horns: face a difficulty boldly
a wet blanket: someone who spoils other people's fun
turn over a new leaf: change your behaviour for the better
at the eleventh hour: at the last possible moment
a bone of contention: the cause of a disagreement
once in a blue moon: very rarely

lesson.title: Ifeanyi decided to take the bull by the horns and report the matter.
steps: Don't picture a real bull. Ask what the whole sentence is about: reporting a matter.
So the idiom means he faced the difficulty boldly.

lesson.text: Exam options usually include one choice that takes the words literally (about real bulls). It is almost always wrong.
Keep a notebook of idioms you meet in novels, newspapers and past comprehension passages, with a sentence of your own for each.

questions.prompt: The two brothers have finally buried the hatchet. This means they have
questions.explanation: To bury the hatchet is to end a quarrel and make peace. "Hidden a weapon" takes the words literally.

questions.prompt: Bola let the cat out of the bag about the surprise party. Bola
questions.explanation: To let the cat out of the bag is to reveal a secret, usually by mistake.

questions.prompt: The candidates burnt the midnight oil before the exam. They
questions.explanation: Burning the midnight oil means working or studying late at night.

questions.prompt: Stop beating about the bush and tell us what happened. The speaker wants the listener to
questions.explanation: Beating about the bush means avoiding the main point, so the speaker wants them to say it directly.

questions.prompt: The land between the two villages has become a bone of contention. The land is
questions.explanation: A bone of contention is something people argue over.
